content.text:
1) Answer

Short answer: You cannot “prove” a person’s state of mind. What you can do is examine whether James Cleverly, while Home Secretary (13 November 2023–5 July 2024), advanced and defended measures that independent courts and human‑rights bodies judged to be incompatible with key human‑rights protections, and whether he proceeded despite those warnings. On that evidence, he did.

Key evidence

- He personally introduced the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Bill on 7 December 2023 and led it through the Commons; it received Royal Assent on 25 April 2024. The Act’s purpose was to enable removal of asylum seekers to Rwanda and to require decision‑makers and UK courts to treat Rwanda as “safe.” ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-policy-statement/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-policy-statement-accessible?utm_source=openai))

- In the Bill’s official ECHR statement, the Minister in charge (James Cleverly) stated he was “unable to make a statement” that the Bill was compatible with Convention rights, yet the government wished Parliament to proceed anyway (a section 19(1)(b) HRA statement). This is an explicit acknowledgment that compatibility could not be certified at introduction. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-draft-bill/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-accessible?utm_source=openai))

- What the legislation did, in brief:
  - Instructed courts and officials to treat Rwanda as safe and sharply limited judicial scrutiny of removals on “general safety” grounds.
  - Disapplied parts of the Human Rights Act 1998.
  - Stated it is for a minister to decide whether to comply with European Court of Human Rights interim measures (Rule 39). These are not my characterizations; they are drawn from the government’s own factsheet. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-factsheets/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-factsheet-accessible?utm_source=openai))

- This legislative strategy directly followed a unanimous UK Supreme Court judgment (15 November 2023) holding the Rwanda removal policy unlawful due to a real risk of refoulement (return to persecution or serious harm), i.e., a violation of Article 3 ECHR and the non‑refoulement principle. ([supremecourt.uk](https://supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2023-0093?utm_source=openai))

- Parliament’s Joint Committee on Human Rights (MPs and peers) concluded the Bill “does not comply with the UK’s human rights obligations and would place the UK in breach of international law,” noting in particular UNHCR’s view that Rwanda was not safe. ([publications.parliament.uk](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/jt5804/jtselect/jtrights/435/summary.html?utm_source=openai))

- The Equality and Human Rights Commission (the UK’s statutory NHRI) warned the Bill “undermines the universality of human rights by disapplying core provisions of the HRA” and risks breaches of the right to life, the prohibition of torture/inhuman or degrading treatment, and the right to an effective remedy. ([equalityhumanrights.com](https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/rights-watchdog-responds-safety-rwanda-bill?utm_source=openai))

- The UN Refugee Agency maintained throughout that the UK‑Rwanda arrangement is not compatible with international refugee law and reiterated concerns even after the new treaty and legislation. UN High Commissioner for Refugees and the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights jointly warned of harmful consequences when the Bill neared passage. ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/uk/what-we-do/uk-asylum-policy-and-illegal-migration-act/uk-rwanda-asylum-partnership?utm_source=openai))

- The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights stated the Bill “raises major issues about the human rights of asylum seekers and the rule of law,” highlighting that it prevents meaningful recourse to UK courts on non‑refoulement and allows ministers to decide whether to comply with Strasbourg interim measures. ([coe.int](https://www.coe.int/en/web/migration-and-refugees/-/serious-human-rights-concerns-about-united-kingdom-s-rwanda-bill?utm_source=openai))

What this shows
- Knowing the Supreme Court’s findings and the objections of UNHCR, the JCHR, the EHRC, and the Council of Europe Commissioner, James Cleverly still introduced, defended and secured passage of legislation that disapplies elements of the HRA, curtails judicial scrutiny, and enables ministers to disregard Rule 39 interim measures. That is strong evidence that, as Home Secretary, he was prepared to press ahead with a policy despite authoritative warnings that it risked violating core human‑rights obligations. Whether one labels that “disregard” is a value judgment; the documentary record supports the claim that he prioritized the policy’s deterrence aims over those human‑rights safeguards. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-draft-bill/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-accessible?utm_source=openai))

Context after his tenure
- After the July 2024 change of government, ministers brought forward legislation to repeal the Safety of Rwanda Act; the repeal clause advanced in early 2025. That later reversal does not alter the record of what Mr Cleverly did while in office. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/Commons/2025-03-11/debates/115e530b-a4f6-4bc2-a1db-1196db8d2b21/BorderSecurityAsylumAndImmigrationBill%28SeventhSitting%29?utm_source=openai))


2) Sources considered TRUSTWORTHY

- Source: UK Supreme Court (supremecourt.uk)
  Reasoning 1: Primary, authoritative court of last resort; publishes judgments and press summaries. 
  Reasoning 2: The AAA judgment is the definitive legal finding on the Rwanda policy’s lawfulness as of 15 November 2023. ([supremecourt.uk](https://supremecourt.uk/cases/uksc-2023-0093?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Legislation.gov.uk (The National Archives)
  Reasoning 1: Official repository for UK legislation; definitive texts and commencement notes.
  Reasoning 2: Confirms the Act’s content, commencement, and legal effect, including the statutory designation of Rwanda as “safe.” ([legislation.gov.uk](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2024/8/enacted?utm_source=openai))

- Source: GOV.UK – Safety of Rwanda Bill factsheet
  Reasoning 1: Official government publication; states the government’s own intent and framing.
  Reasoning 2: Sets out that the Bill disapplies parts of the HRA, restricts interim relief, and gives ministers discretion on Rule 39 measures—core to assessing human‑rights impact. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-factsheets/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-factsheet-accessible?utm_source=openai))

- Source: GOV.UK – Policy statement foreword by the Home Secretary (Jan 11, 2024)
  Reasoning 1: Official ministerial position.
  Reasoning 2: Evidences Mr Cleverly’s personal advocacy and rationale despite the Supreme Court ruling. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-policy-statement/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-policy-statement-accessible?utm_source=openai))

- Source: GOV.UK – Safety of Rwanda Bill (accessible) – ECHR statement
  Reasoning 1: Official text of the Bill and ministerial statements.
  Reasoning 2: Documents the section 19(1)(b) statement that compatibility could not be certified at introduction. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-draft-bill/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-accessible?utm_source=openai))

- Source: UK Parliament – Joint Committee on Human Rights report
  Reasoning 1: Cross‑party parliamentary committee with a mandate to assess rights compliance.
  Reasoning 2: Provides a reasoned conclusion that the Bill does not comply with the UK’s human‑rights obligations. ([publications.parliament.uk](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/jt5804/jtselect/jtrights/435/summary.html?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Equality and Human Rights Commission
  Reasoning 1: Statutory NHRI for Great Britain; independent; recognized by the UN.
  Reasoning 2: Assesses the Bill as risking breaches of fundamental rights and undermining the HRA—directly relevant. ([equalityhumanrights.com](https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/rights-watchdog-responds-safety-rwanda-bill?utm_source=openai))

- Source: UNHCR (United Nations Refugee Agency)
  Reasoning 1: UN authority on refugee protection; expert evidence was relied on by UK courts.
  Reasoning 2: Maintains the arrangement is incompatible with international refugee law; lists formal statements (including 23 April 2024). ([unhcr.org](https://www.unhcr.org/uk/what-we-do/uk-asylum-policy-and-illegal-migration-act/uk-rwanda-asylum-partnership?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights (coe.int)
  Reasoning 1: Regional human‑rights watchdog linked to the ECHR system.
  Reasoning 2: Issues a detailed statement identifying how the Bill curtails judicial scrutiny and engages non‑refoulement concerns. ([coe.int](https://www.coe.int/en/web/migration-and-refugees/-/serious-human-rights-concerns-about-united-kingdom-s-rwanda-bill?utm_source=openai))

- Source: UK Parliament news page on Bill’s passage
  Reasoning 1: Official parliamentary record of legislative stages.
  Reasoning 2: Confirms dates and passage through “ping‑pong” to Royal Assent. ([parliament.uk](https://www.parliament.uk/business/news/2024/march/safety-of-rwanda-asylum-and-immigration-bill-returns-to-the-lords/?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Hansard (UK Parliament)
  Reasoning 1: Verbatim official record of debates.
  Reasoning 2: Shows Mr Cleverly’s own presentation/defence of the Bill and its intent. ([hansard.parliament.uk](https://hansard.parliament.uk/Commons/2023-12-12/debates/FA4DDF9F-19EF-4954-9BFA-6997E4A74E79/SafetyOfRwandaAsylumAndImmigrationBill?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Reuters
  Reasoning 1: International wire service with strong sourcing standards.
  Reasoning 2: Corroborates Royal Assent and UN leaders’ criticisms contemporaneously. ([reuters.com](https://www.reuters.com/world/uk/britains-rwanda-asylum-legislation-formally-becomes-law-2024-04-25/?utm_source=openai))


3) Sources considered NOT TRUSTWORTHY (for this specific question)

- Source: The Sun
  Reasoning 1: Tabloid with a strong editorial slant; not a primary source for complex legal/rights analysis.
  Reasoning 2: Coverage of James Cleverly is often personality‑ or politics‑focused; not suitable to substantiate human‑rights compliance claims. I therefore did not rely on it for this assessment. ([thesun.co.uk](https://www.thesun.co.uk/news/26543034/james-cleverly-swimming-plymouth-johnny-mercer/?utm_source=openai))

- Source: “the-amnesty.com” (blog site, not Amnesty International)
  Reasoning 1: Not the official Amnesty International domain; unclear editorial controls.
  Reasoning 2: Opinionated content without primary documentation; I excluded it in favor of Amnesty International UK’s official materials and institutional reports. ([the-amnesty.com](https://the-amnesty.com/2024/03/17/selective-empathy-and-double-standards-why-the-rwanda-bill-violates-democratic-values/?utm_source=openai))

- Source: Wikipedia (background only)
  Reasoning 1: Useful for orientation but crowd‑edited; not authoritative on contested legal matters.
  Reasoning 2: I did not use Wikipedia to support any contested factual or legal claims; I cross‑checked all dates and legal points with official sources. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_of_Rwanda_%28Asylum_and_Immigration%29_Act_2024?utm_source=openai))

If you want, I can compile a document with the key passages from the cited official sources, aligned to each element of the argument (section 19 statement, Supreme Court findings, limits on judicial review, Rule 39 treatment, and the assessments by UNHCR/EHRC/JCHR).
